titles.Associated appendages: Oil gland, duct and hair muscle

Epidermis.description: The epidermis is the thin outer layer of the skin, made of keratinocytes that rise from the basal layer to the dead, flattened surface and are shed. Melanocytes sit among the basal cells and make the pigment melanin that colours the skin.
clinical: Psoriasis
Keratinocytes turn over far too quickly, so thick, silvery scales build up on the surface of the epidermis. Scalp involvement is common.
Vitiligo
Loss of melanocytes from the basal layer, usually from an autoimmune attack, leaves smooth white patches of skin.
Keloid scar
After injury, the dermis makes excess collagen, forming a raised scar that grows beyond the original wound edge.

Hypodermis.description: The hypodermis is the layer of fat beneath the dermis. In the scalp, tough fibrous septa bind the skin firmly to the galea and carry the larger blood vessels and nerves, while fat lobules fill the spaces between them.
clinical: Heavy scalp bleeding
The fibrous septa hold cut blood vessels open, so scalp wounds bleed heavily.

Galea aponeurotica.description: The galea aponeurotica is a tough, fibrous sheet covering the top of the skull, linking the frontalis muscle at the forehead to the occipitalis muscle at the back of the head. Beneath it lies loose areolar tissue, which lets the scalp slide over the skull.
clinical: Subgaleal haemorrhage
Bleeding into the loose layer under the galea can spread across the whole scalp and cause major blood loss. It is a recognised risk in newborns after vacuum-assisted delivery.

Hair follicle.description: The hair follicle is a pocket in the skin that grows a hair. It holds the hair shaft, the inner and outer root sheaths around it, and the hair bulb, where fast-dividing cells build the hair. The dermal papilla, a cap of connective tissue at the base of the bulb, feeds these cells and helps control hair growth.
clinical: Alopecia areata
The immune system attacks growing (anagen) follicles, causing patchy hair loss. The follicles usually survive, so hair often regrows.
Androgenetic alopecia
Androgens gradually shrink hair follicles (miniaturisation), so hairs become finer and shorter over time.

Follicle context.description: From the outside in, the follicle wall is made of the outer root sheath, which continues from the epidermis, and the inner root sheath, which surrounds the lower hair shaft. At the base, matrix cells divide to make new hair and wrap around the dermal papilla.
clinical: Chemotherapy hair loss
Matrix cells divide rapidly, so cytotoxic drugs damage them and hairs break or fall out during treatment. Hair usually regrows afterwards.

Follicle cellular field.description: The outer root sheath is the outer wall of the hair follicle, and it is continuous with the epidermis above. Its cells are keratinocytes, each with a nucleus surrounded by cytoplasm.

Glands.description: Sebaceous (oil) glands sit beside the follicle and release an oily secretion called sebum into its upper part, which lubricates the skin and hair. Eccrine sweat glands are coiled tubes deep in the dermis and hypodermis that make watery sweat, which a duct carries up to the surface. The arrector pili, a tiny muscle attached to each follicle, pulls the hair upright when it contracts.
clinical: Acne
Sebaceous glands make excess sebum, which can block the follicle with keratin and bacteria, forming spots.
Cystic fibrosis
A faulty CFTR channel in the sweat duct stops salt being reabsorbed, so sweat is unusually salty; the sweat chloride test uses this to diagnose the condition.

Associated appendages.description: The sebaceous gland drains through a short duct into the upper part of the hair follicle, releasing sebum. The arrector pili is a tiny smooth muscle attached to the follicle; when it contracts it pulls the hair upright, which causes goosebumps.

Vessels & nerves.description: The scalp's blood supply forms two networks: a deep plexus at the junction of the dermis and fat that feeds the follicles and glands, and a subpapillary plexus that gives each papilla a capillary loop. Free nerve endings sense pain and temperature, nerve endings wrapped around each hair follicle detect hair movement, and cutaneous nerves carry these signals to the brain or spinal cord.
clinical: Shingles
Varicella-zoster virus reactivates in a sensory nerve ganglion and travels down one cutaneous nerve, causing a painful, one-sided band of blisters.

Sensory receptors.description: Pacinian corpuscles are onion-shaped sensors in the deep dermis and hypodermis. Layers of flattened cells around the nerve ending filter out steady pressure, so the corpuscle responds mainly to quick vibration and changes in pressure.
clinical: Loss of vibration sense
Vibration sense, tested with a 128 Hz tuning fork, is an early sign of peripheral neuropathy such as diabetic neuropathy.

Unit restoration covers.description: These are thin model-only overlays that sit over the follicle parts and the sebaceous duct wall, keeping their outlines continuous. They are not separate anatomy; the tissue beneath is described under the follicle and gland entries.

Cell restoration covers.description: These are thin model-only overlays that sit over the outer root sheath cells so each cell looks whole. They are not cells in their own right; the real cells are described under Outer root sheath cells.

Reconstructed teaching context.description: A model-only piece that joins the arrector pili muscle to the papillary dermis, the upper layer of the dermis. In real skin the muscle is anchored in this layer; this piece only approximates that connection and is not a separate structure.

parts.description: The stratum corneum is the outermost layer of the epidermis, made of about 15–20 layers of dead, flattened, nucleus-free cells called corneocytes in thick skin. Each corneocyte is packed with keratin filaments set in a filaggrin matrix and enclosed by a tough envelope, and the cells are glued together by lipids from the granular layer below. This layer is the skin's main water barrier and is shed continuously as skin flakes. In sections it is the pale pink, anucleate band at the top of the epidermis.

The stratum granulosum is the layer of flattened cells, one to three layers thick in thin skin and three to five in thick skin, lying just beneath the stratum corneum. Its cells contain dark, basophilic keratohyalin granules (profilaggrin and loricrin) and lamellar bodies that release lipid to seal the barrier. The cells lose their nuclei and organelles as they die here, and the dark granules make this layer easy to recognise in sections. Loss-of-function mutations in the filaggrin gene cause ichthyosis vulgaris and predispose to atopic eczema.

The stratum spinosum is the thick middle layer of living epidermis, made of several layers of polyhedral keratinocytes (keratin-making skin cells) joined by many desmosomes (cell-to-cell anchoring junctions). Fixation pulls the cells apart at these junctions, leaving small spines that give the layer its name, and the cells are rich in keratin filaments. Dendritic Langerhans cells, which present antigens to T cells, sit among them. Pemphigus vulgaris autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 split this layer, causing blisters.

The stratum basale (germinativum) is the single row of cuboidal to columnar cells resting on the basement membrane at the base of the epidermis. It holds the stem cells that renew the epidermis, and each cell is anchored to the membrane by hemidesmosomes. Its undersurface forms rete ridges that interlock with the dermal papillae. Melanocytes and Merkel cells are scattered among these cells, and a new keratinocyte takes about 4 weeks to reach the surface and be shed.

Melanocytes are pigment-producing cells of neural-crest origin that lie among the basal cells, roughly one for every ten basal keratinocytes. Their branching dendrites reach up between the spinous cells and pass melanin-filled packets (melanosomes) to about 36 keratinocytes each, forming the epidermal melanin unit. Their pigment caps sit over the nucleus of each keratinocyte they supply to shield its DNA from ultraviolet light. Skin colour depends on the amount and type of melanin transferred, not on the number of melanocytes, and melanoma arises from these cells.

The papillary dermis is the thin upper layer of the dermis, lying directly beneath the epidermis, where it forms the dermal papillae that interlock with the epidermal rete ridges. It is loose connective tissue containing fine type I and III collagen, oxytalan (fine elastic) fibres, fibroblasts and mast cells. Its capillary loops nourish the avascular epidermis, and many sensory nerve endings sit here. The interlocking papillae help the skin resist shearing forces between the epidermis and dermis.

The reticular dermis is the thick, deep part of the dermis, made of dense irregular connective tissue with coarse type I collagen bundles and thick elastic fibres. These give the skin its tensile strength and recoil, and this layer holds the hair follicles, sweat and sebaceous glands, and the deeper blood vessels and nerves. The main direction of its collagen bundles gives Langer's cleavage lines, and tears in this layer form stretch marks (striae). In sections it stains as dense, pink, interwoven collagen.

The fibrous septa of the hypodermis are tough partitions of connective tissue that run down from the dermis through the subcutaneous fat, dividing it into lobules. In the scalp they bind the skin firmly to the galea aponeurotica beneath, and they carry the larger blood vessels and nerves to the skin. In sections they show as dense bands of pink collagen cutting through the pale fat.

Adipose lobules are the clusters of fat cells (adipocytes) that fill the hypodermis between the fibrous septa. Each adipocyte stores energy as one large fat droplet that pushes its nucleus to the edge; the fat dissolves during slide preparation, so the cells look clear and empty in sections, giving a signet-ring appearance. The lobules also provide insulation and cushioning for the scalp.

The hair shaft is the part of the hair that grows out of the follicle, a column of dead, hardened (keratinised) cells made by the hair matrix at the base of the follicle. It has an outer cuticle of overlapping scales, a thicker cortex containing melanin pigment that gives hair its colour, and, in some hairs, a central medulla. In sections it is the innermost core of the follicle, surrounded by the inner root sheath in its lower part.

The inner root sheath is a tube of epithelial cells that wraps the growing hair from the bulb up to the sebaceous duct. It has three layers (cuticle, Huxley's layer and Henle's layer) whose cells interlock with the hair and help shape it as it grows. The inner root sheath breaks down at the level of the sebaceous duct, so it is seen only in the lower follicle. In sections it appears as a ring of cells between the hair shaft and the outer root sheath.

The outer root sheath is the outer wall of the hair follicle, lying just inside the glassy membrane that separates it from the dermis. Its cells are pale and glycogen-rich, and they do not keratinise, unlike the inner root sheath and hair within it. It runs the full length of the follicle, from the follicle mouth down to the hair bulb.

The hair bulb is the swollen, cup-shaped base of the follicle that caps the dermal papilla. Its matrix cells divide very rapidly to form the hair shaft and inner root sheath, and melanocytes among them supply pigment to the hair. It is the widest part of the lower follicle, with a dome of matrix cells over the papilla. Because matrix cells divide so quickly, chemotherapy often causes hair loss.

keys: Dermal papilla of hair – retained units
parts.description: The dermal papilla is a small cone of specialised fibroblast-like cells at the core of the hair bulb, supplied by capillaries. It sends signals to the overlying matrix cells that help control when a follicle starts, continues and stops growing a hair in the hair cycle. In sections it appears as a pale, loosely packed cluster of cells in the centre of the bulb, around which the matrix cells are arranged.

Sebaceous glands are small sacs of fat-producing cells (sebocytes) that open into the upper part of each hair follicle and release sebum, an oily lipid mixture that lubricates the skin and hair. They are holocrine glands, meaning the cells fill with lipid, then disintegrate to release the secretion. They are absent from the palms and soles. In sections they look like clusters of pale, foamy cells with small, dark nuclei at the edges, and blocked ducts underlie acne.

The arrector pili is a tiny bundle of smooth muscle fibres that runs obliquely from the connective tissue sheath of each hair follicle up to the papillary dermis. It is supplied by sympathetic nerves, and when it contracts it pulls the hair upright and produces goose bumps. In sections it appears as a thin band of pink smooth muscle cells beside the follicle, often close to the sebaceous gland.

The eccrine secretory coil is the coiled, deep end of an eccrine sweat gland, lying in the lower dermis and hypodermis. It produces a watery secretion, sweat, which cools the body as it evaporates. Its wall contains clear secretory cells, darker cells and an outer layer of myoepithelial cells that contract to push sweat towards the duct. In sections the coil appears as a cluster of round profiles with a wide, open lumen.

The eccrine sweat duct is a narrow tube carrying sweat from the coil up through the dermis and epidermis to the surface. Its wall has two layers of small cuboidal cells that reabsorb sodium and chloride, so the sweat reaching the surface is less salty. In sections it is smaller than the coil, with a narrow lumen, and in the epidermis it spirals up to open at a pore. Defective chloride reabsorption here is why sweat chloride is raised in cystic fibrosis.

Cutaneous arterioles are small muscular arteries that carry blood into the skin from the deep vascular plexus at the dermis-hypodermis junction, then rise through the reticular dermis to supply the subpapillary plexus. Their thick smooth muscle walls are controlled by sympathetic nerves, so they narrow to conserve heat and widen to lose it. In sections they are small round vessels with thick muscular walls and a narrow lumen, unlike thin-walled veins.

Venules are the small veins of the skin that collect blood from the capillary loops and drain it into the subpapillary and deep venous plexuses. The postcapillary venules, the thin-walled vessels just beyond the capillaries, are the main site where leukocytes (white blood cells) leave the blood during inflammation. In sections they have a wider lumen and thinner wall than arterioles, and they often contain blood cells.

The subpapillary plexus is a horizontal network of arterioles and venules lying just beneath the papillary dermis, at its junction with the reticular dermis. It gives off a capillary loop to each dermal papilla, and its venous part acts as a large blood reservoir that helps regulate heat loss. In sections it shows as a band of small vessels running parallel to the skin surface, below the dermal papillae.

Papillary capillary loops are the hairpin-shaped capillaries that rise into each dermal papilla from the subpapillary plexus and return to it. They bring oxygen and nutrients to the epidermis, which has no blood vessels of its own, by diffusion across the thin basement membrane. In sections the loops appear as tiny channels, often filled with red blood cells, in the upper part of the papillae.

Cutaneous nerves are bundles of myelinated and unmyelinated fibres that supply the skin, running in the deep dermis and hypodermis alongside the deep vascular plexus. They carry sensory fibres from skin receptors, and sympathetic fibres to the sweat glands, arterioles and arrector pili muscles. Smaller branches rise into the papillary dermis to reach the touch corpuscles (Meissner's) and free nerve endings. In sections each nerve shows several fascicles (bundles of axons), each wrapped in a tough sheath called the perineurium, all enclosed by the epineurium.

Free nerve endings are the bare terminal branches of thin sensory axons (Aδ and C fibres) that detect pain, temperature and itch. After losing their Schwann cell covering near the basement membrane, these fine axon branches run between the keratinocytes of the epidermis and in the papillary dermis. They are the most widespread cutaneous receptors. In sections they are hard to see in routine stains and are revealed by silver or immunostaining.

Hair follicle nerve endings are sensory endings that wrap around the lower part of each hair follicle, below the sebaceous gland. They include longitudinal lanceolate endings that run along the follicle and circumferential endings that encircle it. These rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors fire when the hair is bent, making them important for light touch on hairy skin. In silver-stained sections they look like fine axons coiled around the follicle.

The Pacinian axon terminal is the bare, unmyelinated end of a large sensory axon at the centre of a Pacinian corpuscle. The myelin sheath stops where the axon enters the inner core, which is formed by flattened cells wrapped around the terminal. When the surrounding lamellae are squeezed, the terminal membrane is stretched, opening ion channels that trigger a nerve impulse. In sections it appears as a small axon profile at the very centre of the concentric layers.

The outer root sheath is the continuous outer epithelial wall of the hair follicle, running from the epidermis at the follicle mouth down to the hair bulb. It is continuous with the basal layer of the epidermis, and the follicle's stem cells sit within it at a bulge near the arrector pili attachment. In sections it appears as the outermost ring of follicle epithelium, separated from the dermis by the glassy membrane.

keys: Outer root sheath bulk continuity longitudinal restoration cover
parts.description: The outer root sheath is the outer epithelial wall of the hair follicle, a continuous sleeve of keratinocytes (skin cells that make keratin) running from the epidermis down the follicle. At the mouth of the follicle its cells are continuous with the basal layer of the epidermis, so the follicle is effectively an inward extension of the skin surface. In a section it forms the outermost band of follicle epithelium, lying between the surrounding dermal connective tissue and the inner root sheath.

Outer root sheath cell cytoplasm is the cytoplasm of the keratinocytes that form the outer wall of the hair follicle, the material that fills each cell around its nucleus. It contains a dense network of keratin filaments, which give these cells strength and link them to their neighbours through desmosomes (small attachment junctions). In the lower follicle the cytoplasm often looks pale, because these cells store glycogen, a reserve of sugar.

parts.description: The cytoplasm of outer root sheath cells is the working interior of each keratinocyte, lying between its nucleus and its cell membrane in the follicle wall. It holds ribosomes for making protein and mitochondria for producing energy, which keep the cell active. Because these cells are continuous with the basal layer of the epidermis, they share the basic cell structure of skin keratinocytes.

The outer root sheath cell nucleus is the round to oval, membrane-bound compartment in each keratinocyte of the outer follicle wall that houses the cell's DNA. It sits near the middle of the cell and takes up haematoxylin (the blue nuclear stain) strongly, so nuclei show as dark blue dots in haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections. Counting these nuclei across the wall gives a quick sense of how many cell layers the outer root sheath has at that level.

parts.description: Outer root sheath nuclei are the DNA-carrying nuclei of the keratinocytes lining the follicle wall, each enclosed by a double nuclear envelope. In a section they appear as oval, blue-staining profiles set within the cytoplasm of the outer wall. Look for the darker nucleolus inside each nucleus, the site where ribosome subunits are assembled.

The inner root sheath is an epithelial sheath that lies between the outer root sheath and the hair shaft, growing down from the hair matrix and enclosing the lower part of the hair. It has three layers, starting next to the hair with a thin cuticle of flat cells that interlocks with the hair, then Huxley's and Henle's layers further out. It breaks down at about the level where the sebaceous duct opens, so in a section it is seen only in the lower follicle.

keys: Inner root sheath bulk continuity longitudinal restoration cover
parts.description: Inner root sheath tissue is the inner epithelial layer of the follicle that wraps the growing hair, and it is made continuously by the matrix below. Its cuticle is a single layer of flattened cells whose edges overlap and interlock with the scales of the hair itself. In a section it appears as a narrow band of cells alongside the hair shaft in the lower follicle, fading away higher up.

Inner root sheath cell cytoplasm is the cell interior of the epithelial cells forming the inner sheath around the growing hair. It is filled with keratin filaments, and in Huxley's layer it also contains trichohyalin granules, dense protein granules that help cross-link the filaments and stiffen the sheath. Huxley's layer is recognised partly by these granules.

parts.description: The cytoplasm of inner root sheath cells is the working interior of these epithelial cells, sitting between their nuclei and cell membranes in the sheath that hugs the hair. It contains keratin filaments and ribosomes, and as the cells move upward they keratinise and then break down. In a section it forms the narrow band of cells lining the hair shaft.

The inner root sheath nucleus is the round to oval, DNA-containing compartment of each cell in the inner sheath that wraps the hair shaft. It stains dark with haematoxylin, the blue nuclear dye, so nuclei stand out in sections of the lower follicle. Because the sheath breaks down near the opening of the sebaceous duct, these nuclei disappear higher up, which helps you judge the level of a section.

parts.description: An inner root sheath nucleus holds the chromosomes of an epithelial cell in the inner sheath, enclosed by a nuclear envelope pierced with pores. In sections these nuclei are oval and blue, lined up in a narrow band that hugs the hair shaft. Recognising this band by its nuclei helps separate the inner sheath from the outer root sheath, which lies further out.

The hair matrix is the zone of rapidly dividing cells at the base of the hair bulb (the swollen root of the follicle), wrapping around the dermal papilla. Matrix cells divide continuously and move upwards, producing the hair shaft and the inner root sheath. The matrix is one of the fastest-dividing tissues in the body, and in a section it appears as a dense, blue-staining cap at the base of the bulb.

keys: Hair matrix bulk continuity longitudinal restoration cover
parts.description: Hair matrix tissue is the actively growing base of the hair follicle, where a ring of closely packed cells surrounds the dermal papilla. Cell divisions (mitoses) are common here in a growing (anagen) follicle, which is why the region looks crowded and dark blue. Its cells give rise to every part of the hair shaft and the inner root sheath, so the matrix is the engine of hair growth.

Hair matrix cell cytoplasm is the cell interior of the dividing cells at the base of the follicle, and it is packed with free ribosomes. These ribosomes are rich in RNA, which takes up the blue dye haematoxylin, so the cytoplasm looks basophilic (blue-staining) in haematoxylin and eosin sections. As the cells move upwards they fill with the tough keratin of hair and lose this blue colour.

parts.description: The cytoplasm of hair matrix cells is the cell body of the rapidly dividing cells that make hair, lying around the nucleus and close to the dermal papilla. It contains many ribosomes and mitochondria, which power the cell's fast protein production. As these cells move upward and keratinise, their cytoplasm is converted into the tough keratin of the hair, and the cells flatten and die.

The hair matrix cell nucleus is the round, DNA-bearing nucleus of each dividing cell at the base of the hair follicle. Because the matrix is so active, its nuclei are often seen in mitosis, with the chromosomes condensed into dark, rod-like threads. Nuclei here are tightly packed around the dermal papilla, so their dense crowding at the base of the bulb helps you recognise the active matrix.

parts.description: The nucleus of a hair matrix cell is the membrane-bound compartment holding the cell's chromosomes and the nucleolus, where ribosome subunits are assembled. Before a matrix cell divides, its DNA is duplicated inside this nucleus, so the nucleus is rich in DNA and stains intensely. In a section these nuclei are the dark, round to oval spots within the blue-staining cells at the base of the bulb.

The hair shaft is the hair fibre itself, a column of hard keratin (the tough protein of hair and nails) made by cells from the hair matrix. In a section most of the shaft is cortex, which gives the hair its bulk and pigment, with a thin cuticle of overlapping scales at its edge; some hairs also have a central medulla. Its cells are dead and keratinised, so they stain pink with eosin and form a pink column up the centre of the follicle.

The hair shaft is the keratinised fibre that grows up through the follicle and out of the skin, produced continuously by the hair matrix. Its outer cuticle is a sheet of flat, overlapping scale cells that interlock with the cuticle of the inner root sheath, which helps anchor the growing hair in its follicle. In a section, most of the shaft is the cortex, and the thin, scaly edge is the cuticle; a central medulla may be seen in thicker hairs.

The dermal papilla is a small, rounded cluster of specialised connective tissue cells at the base of the hair bulb, enclosed by the hair matrix. It has a rich capillary (tiny blood vessel) supply and sends signals to the matrix cells, which control when and how the hair grows. In a section it appears as a loosely packed knob of cells sitting at the centre of the bulb, with the matrix wrapped around it.

Dermal papilla tissue is the core of connective tissue cells (fibroblasts) at the base of each hair bulb, a specialised part of the dermis that reaches up into the follicle. Its cells release growth signals that tell the surrounding matrix to divide, and its capillaries bring blood to the growing bulb. Identify it as the cell-rich knob inside the bulb, with matrix cells surrounding it on all sides except its base.

The sebaceous gland is a small, sac-like gland in the dermis that opens through a short duct into the upper part of a hair follicle, releasing sebum, an oily lipid mixture. Its cells fill with lipid and then break down as they are shed, a mode of secretion called holocrine secretion. In a section the gland looks foamy and pale, because the lipid dissolves away during processing and leaves clear spaces in the cells.

The arrector pili is a small bundle of smooth muscle that runs from the connective tissue sheath of a hair follicle obliquely up to the papillary dermis, the thin upper layer of the dermis. When it contracts it pulls the follicle upright, raising the hair and producing the goosebumps (cutis anserina) of cold or fear. It is supplied by sympathetic nerves, and in a section it looks like a pink band of smooth muscle beside the follicle, angled up towards the skin surface.

The hair matrix papillary apposition is the zone where matrix cells lie directly against the dermal papilla, so they sit closest to its signals. The papilla sends signals that control how fast these matrix cells divide and how they mature into hair. In a section it is the dense, blue-staining ring of matrix cells that wraps around the papilla.

keys: Hair matrix papillary apposition longitudinal restoration cover
parts.description: Hair matrix papillary apposition is the contact layer where rapidly dividing matrix cells cling to the surface of the dermal papilla at the base of the bulb. Cells here take their instructions from the papilla beneath them, and they move upward as they differentiate into hair shaft and inner root sheath. In a bulb section, look for the densely packed, blue-staining layer hugging the papilla.

The sebaceous infundibular duct wall is the lining of the infundibulum, the funnel-shaped upper part of a hair follicle that runs from the skin surface down to where the sebaceous gland duct opens. It is keratinising stratified squamous epithelium (layered, flat-celled skin lining), continuous with the epidermis, so in a section it looks like skin with layered cells and a keratin surface. Look for the sebaceous gland opening into this lined segment.

keys: Sebaceous infundibular duct wall restoration cover
parts.description: The wall of the infundibulum, the funnel-shaped upper follicle where the sebaceous gland empties, is a thin epithelial lining continuous with the epidermis. This lining is layered skin epithelium that keeps producing keratin, so its cells look like epidermal cells in a section. Its job is to form a passage that lets sebum reach the skin surface alongside the hair.

The papillary dermal attachment is the point where the arrector pili muscle anchors into the papillary dermis, the thin upper layer of the dermis just beneath the epidermis. The papillary dermis is loose connective tissue with fine collagen fibres, and this anchorage lets the muscle pull the hair follicle upright when it contracts. In a section, look for the oblique smooth muscle bundle that ends in the upper dermis, close to the epidermal border.
